title: How Much Does It Cost to Seal a Driveway? $0.10-$0.50/Sq Ft
h1: How Much Does It Cost to Seal a Driveway?
query: how much does it cost to seal a driveway
keywords: how much to seal coat a driveway
average cost to seal a driveway
description: Sealing a driveway costs about $0.10-$0.30 per sq ft DIY and $0.20-$0.50 hired, so a 2-car drive runs roughly $100-$450. Line items and quote tips.
dek: Sealing a driveway costs about $0.10-$0.30 per sq ft DIY and $0.20-$0.50 hired, so a 2-car drive runs roughly $100-$450.
intro: It costs about $0.10 to $0.30 per square foot to seal an asphalt driveway yourself and roughly $0.20 to $0.50 per square foot to hire a sealcoating crew, based on typical retail material prices and the rates contractors commonly quote at the time of writing. For a two-car driveway of about 800 square feet, that works out to roughly $100 to $250 in DIY materials or $200 to $450 hired.

The real choice is usually a weekend plus a couple hundred dollars of sealer against a bill that runs two to three times higher. Either can be right. Driveway size, the amount of crack repair and the value of your time decide it. Below are the line items, what moves a quote up or down, and the long-run math.
quickAnswer: Plan on roughly $0.10 to $0.30 per square foot for DIY materials (two coats) and $0.20 to $0.50 per square foot for a contractor, with many crews charging a minimum of around $150 to $300 per job. Crack repair is often extra. Budget for a fresh coat every two to three years, not every year. These are broad national ranges; local prices vary.

sections.h: How Much Does It Cost to Seal a Driveway? at a Glance

head: Cost item
Typical range at the time of writing
rows: Roughly $100 to $250 plus $30 to $60 in tools

blocks.p: Those figures assume an asphalt driveway in reasonable shape that mostly needs cleaning, some crack filling and two coats. A driveway with widespread cracking, potholes or sunken patches is a different job, and the repairs can cost more than the sealing.

Timing matters too. Paying to coat blacktop that was laid this summer wastes money and can trap oils the pavement still needs to release; see [when to seal a new asphalt driveway](/when-should-you-seal-a-new-asphalt-driveway/) for the wait. And if you are still deciding whether to seal at all, start with [should asphalt driveways be sealed](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/).

sections.h: What Does It Cost to Seal a Driveway Yourself?

blocks.p: Sealer is the biggest expense. Retail 5-gallon pails of water-based asphalt emulsion commonly sell for roughly $25 to $60 at the time of writing, with basic emulsions at the low end and rubberized or polymer-modified formulas at the top. Each pail typically covers about 250 to 400 square feet per coat, so a two-coat job depends heavily on whether your driveway drinks sealer or lets it spread.
The low numbers pair a tight surface with budget sealer; the high numbers pair a rough surface with premium sealer. Most driveways land in the middle.

Crack filler adds roughly $10 to $25 per jug or a few dollars per caulk tube, and a neglected driveway can use three or four jugs. An oil spot primer adds $10 to $20. A squeegee-brush, edging brush, painter's tape and drill mixing paddle come to roughly $30 to $70 the first time, and most of that is reusable.

Expect most of a weekend for a two-car driveway, counting cleaning, crack work, two coats and cleanup. Our [best asphalt driveway sealer](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list covers budget and premium pails so you can price both ends.

Residential sealcoating companies usually price by the square foot and then apply a minimum so a small job still covers travel and setup. That minimum is commonly about $150 to $300. Above it, many quotes for cleaning plus two coats fall between $0.20 and $0.50 per square foot. Crews with spray rigs coat open stretches quickly, which is why per-foot rates often drop on bigger jobs.

Contractors usually price crack work separately, by the linear foot or as a flat add-on. Professional crews typically use hot-pour rubberized sealant melted in a kettle, which bonds and flexes better than most retail cold-pour fillers. Rates vary widely by region and crack width, from under a dollar to a few dollars per linear foot. A few short cracks might add $25 to $75; long, branching cracks can add a few hundred.

Spring and early summer are the busiest months. Booking in late summer or early fall, while temperatures are still in range, can sometimes mean a better price or a shorter wait. Some companies discount when neighbors book the same day.
Be wary of anyone going door to door with material left over from a nearby job and a same-day deal. It is a well-known setup for a watered-down product or a sloppy job.
Cleaning, crack treatment, the sealer type, the number of coats and the cure time. A quote that lists only a total and a date leaves out what decides how long the job lasts.

sections.h: How Much Does It Cost to Seal a Concrete Driveway?

blocks.p: Concrete runs on different chemistry, so the numbers differ. Typical DIY material costs at the time of writing run roughly $0.15 to $0.40 per square foot for a penetrating silane-siloxane sealer and roughly $0.15 to $0.35 per square foot for a solvent acrylic, depending on product and region.

blocks.h3: Why the longer interval changes the math

blocks.p: A penetrating concrete sealer is commonly rated for five years or more per its label, while an acrylic film usually needs recoating every two to three years. Even when the gallon price is higher, the penetrating product can cost less per year of protection.

Concrete sealer goes on with a pump sprayer and roller rather than squeegees and mixing paddles, so the one-time tool cost is modest. The main extra on a concrete job is joint and crack sealant, which keeps water out of the base.

Some penetrating sealers ship as concentrates. Compare them by the cost per finished gallon after dilution, not by the price on the jug. For product picks, see the [best concrete driveway sealer](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) list.

sections.h: What Factors Change the Cost of Sealing a Driveway?

blocks.h3: Size, but not in a straight line

blocks.p: Small driveways cost more per square foot because minimum charges and fixed setup, edging and cleanup time get spread over less area. Very large driveways often cost less per foot because spray equipment covers open stretches fast. A long, narrow drive with many edges and turns takes more hand work than a simple rectangle of the same area.

Oil stains need degreasing and priming, and many cracks mean more filler or hot-pour sealant. Badly oxidized gray asphalt absorbs more sealer, pushing material use toward the low end of the coverage range. Potholes and crumbling edges bring a separate patching charge, and patching with hot mix asphalt costs considerably more than sealing.

It matters less than people expect. Moving from a basic emulsion to a premium polymer-modified sealer may add only a few cents per square foot to a contractor bid, and it can extend the life of the coat. In areas where coal tar is restricted, contractors quote asphalt emulsion or acrylic instead.

Labor rates in high-cost metro areas push quotes to the top of the range; rural areas often sit at the bottom. In the North the season is short, so demand bunches up in late spring and summer. In the South the season is longer, but crews often work early mornings to avoid flash-drying on hot pavement. Our guide to the [minimum temperature for sealing a driveway](/what-temperature-to-seal-driveway/) explains the weather limits that shape each region's season.

sections.h: Is It Cheaper to Seal a Driveway Yourself or Hire a Pro?

blocks.p: DIY is clearly cheaper for a typical suburban driveway in decent shape. You can usually save a couple hundred dollars on an 800-square-foot driveway, and the tools carry over to the next round. The work is physical but not technical: clean, fill cracks, spread thin coats.

A very large, steep or long driveway can turn hand-squeegeeing into a two-weekend project. Heavy crack work is another reason, since professional hot-pour sealant generally outlasts retail cold-pour filler and a crew finishes in hours. Physical limits, or simply not wanting sealer on your shoes, are fair reasons too.

Past roughly 1,500 square feet, contractor bulk pricing often lands close to the cost of a stack of premium retail pails. At 2,000 square feet and up, the hired job can be the cheaper option outright once you count the extra pails a porous surface needs.

Some homeowners hire a crew for hot-pour crack sealing only and apply the sealer coats themselves. That puts professional work on the part that matters most for keeping water out while keeping the cheaper DIY labor on the coating. Many crews offer crack-only service, especially outside peak season.
Whichever route you take, the outcome depends on the same fundamentals: a clean, dry surface, cracks filled first, weather in range and thin coats.

sections.h: How Do You Compare Driveway Sealcoating Quotes?

blocks.p: Line them up and list the same items for each: square footage, cleaning method, crack treatment and its price, sealer type, number of coats, application method and cure time. A quote that is much cheaper usually skips something, most often the second coat, the crack work or the cleaning. A one-coat spray job can look great on day one and wear through in the tire lanes by next year.

Contractors sometimes estimate from the street. Measure your driveway yourself, length times width for each section, and compare. If crack sealing is priced by the linear foot, ask for the estimated footage, so you can compare a lower rate against a higher one that assumes fewer feet.

Overspray on concrete, brick or siding is a common complaint with spray rigs, so ask how the crew masks or hand-applies near those surfaces. Ask what happens if rain arrives on the scheduled day and confirm there is no rescheduling fee. Reputable outfits will not seal on a marginal day.

Look for local reviews and a business address. A legitimate contractor gives a written estimate, names the product, carries liability insurance and does not ask for full payment up front. Ask whether they will touch up peeling or missed spots within the first season.

sections.h: Is Driveway Sealing Worth the Cost Over Time?

blocks.p: On sound pavement, usually. Sealing is maintenance, so the comparison is against resurfacing or replacing the driveway early, which costs many times more per square foot. Even a few extra years of surface life can cover a decade of sealing at DIY prices, although the exact benefit depends on climate, traffic and construction quality.

blocks.h3: Seal every two to three years, not every year

blocks.p: That interval is where the math works best. Annual sealing roughly doubles the long-run cost and builds up layers that crack and flake. Many driveways that still bead water after two years can wait another season.

blocks.h3: Crack filling pays back the most

blocks.p: Water entering through open cracks undermines the base and leads to potholes and settling. If money is tight, fill cracks this year and seal next year rather than sealing over open cracks now.

blocks.h3: Skip it on a failing driveway

blocks.p: If more than about a quarter of the surface shows alligator cracking, or there are many potholes and sunken areas, put the money toward resurfacing. Sealing over that damage looks better for a season and does nothing for the base.
Sealing does not add measurable resale value the way a remodel can, but a dark, crack-free driveway signals a maintained property, which is why many sellers reseal a few weeks before listing.

mistakes: Comparing sealer by the pail, not the square foot

A cheap pail that covers 250 square feet can cost more per foot than a pricier one rated for 400. Divide the price by the label coverage before comparing, and use the low end of the coverage range for an old, porous driveway, since rough surfaces soak up more.
Taking the lowest quote without reading it

The cheapest bid often drops a coat, skips crack work or uses a thinned product. Compare quotes line by line on cleaning, crack treatment, sealer type, coats and cure time. A contractor who will not name the product or coat count is a warning sign, not a bargain.
Leaving crack repair out of the budget

Sealer is the visible part of the job, but crack filling keeps water out of the base. Budgeting only for pails leaves cracks open under the fresh coat, and they reappear after one winter. Price the crack filler or hot-pour service first, then add the sealing.
Sealing every year out of habit

Annual sealing roughly doubles the long-run cost compared with a two-to-three-year cycle, and extra layers can crack and peel. Do a water test each spring instead. If water still beads on the surface, the existing coat is working and the money can wait.
Paying to seal a failing driveway

Sealer cannot fix alligator cracking, potholes or a sinking base. A fresh coat on pavement that needs resurfacing buys a season of better looks and nothing else. Get an honest assessment of the structure first, and put the money toward repairs if the base is the problem.
bottomLine: Sealing a typical asphalt driveway yourself costs roughly $0.10 to $0.30 per square foot in materials, about a third to a half of a contractor bid, and the tools carry over to the next round. Hiring out at roughly $0.20 to $0.50 per square foot earns its price on very large driveways, heavy crack repair and for anyone who would rather keep the weekend. Either way, put money into crack repair and a proper second coat before a premium pail, budget for a fresh coat every two to three years, skip sealing on a structurally failing driveway, and compare quotes line by line rather than by total.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to seal a 2-car driveway?
faqs.a: A two-car driveway of roughly 600 to 900 square feet typically costs about $100 to $300 in materials if you do it yourself, including sealer, crack filler and basic tools. Hiring a contractor commonly runs about $200 to $450, more with heavy crack repair. Prices vary by region and by how porous the existing surface is.

faqs.q: What is the average price for sealcoating a driveway?
faqs.a: Contractors commonly quote about $0.20 to $0.50 per square foot for cleaning and two coats, with a minimum charge of roughly $150 to $300 on small jobs. For a typical 800-square-foot driveway that lands around $200 to $450. Crack sealing is often priced separately by the linear foot.

faqs.q: What is the driveway sealing cost per square foot?
faqs.a: About $0.10 to $0.30 per square foot for DIY materials covering two coats on asphalt, and about $0.20 to $0.50 per square foot for a contractor. Concrete penetrating sealers run roughly $0.15 to $0.40 per square foot in materials. Small driveways cost more per foot because of minimum charges.

faqs.q: How many pails of sealer do I need?
faqs.a: Divide the driveway area by the label coverage, then double it for two coats. Most asphalt sealers list roughly 250 to 400 square feet per 5-gallon pail per coat, so an 800-square-foot driveway at 300 square feet per pail needs about six pails. Use the lower figure for rough, gray pavement and buy one spare.

faqs.q: Why are some sealcoating quotes so cheap?
faqs.a: Very low quotes usually skip something: the second coat, crack sealing, a thorough cleaning or full-strength product. Some traveling crews water down sealer to stretch it. Ask each contractor to put the product name, number of coats, crack treatment and cure time in writing, and compare those items rather than the total alone.

faqs.q: Is professional sealcoating worth the extra cost?
faqs.a: It can be for large or badly cracked driveways, or when you lack the time or physical ability to do the work. Crews use hot-pour crack sealant and spray equipment that are hard to match at home. For a typical suburban driveway in good shape, careful DIY work with a quality sealer performs similarly for much less money.

faqs.q: How often should I budget for driveway sealing?
faqs.a: Plan on resealing roughly every two to three years and confirm with a water test before spending. Driveways in harsh sun or heavy freeze-thaw climates may need the shorter end; lightly used driveways in mild climates can sometimes go longer. Sealing every year usually adds cost without adding protection.
